b:
My mother,
who carried me ten months
not as a burden
but as a joy

For a quarter of a century
you have carried me,
in your heart
and in your lap

When
do you intend
to put
me down?

Even on your deathbed
would you answer
"No"?

From the time
I began in the womb,
count the minutes
you have closed your eyes:
even the hands of the clock
would stare in wonder

Though the world held
many comforts for you to enjoy,
you ate whatever food was left over,
and at dusk
when I asked for a snack,
you cooked something fresh for me

Why do you love me
so much?
Because I was born
of your blood?
Am I not
the one
who drank
your blood
to grow
my body?

When I was mocked
and fell
like a refugee,
you were my first
Bharathi,
who gave me courage
without knowing Tamil poetry

Even today
when I have a headache
my mind
searches by itself
for your
tender hands

When I studied
for an exam, well fed,
you stayed hungry
and kept a fast

Your stomach ulcers
point at me
as the culprit

When they said, "an only child,
how spoiled he must be,"
when they said, "having him at this age,
how will she ever raise him?",
you stood silent
like a simpleton;
let my words today
answer for
your silence

What is left
for you still to do?
Wait until the elders
accept me as a learned man?
Let Valluvar be;
he finished his life.
At least now
begin to live yours

Let the mothers
who rise first
and sleep last
die out
with your generation

Hold my hands tightly;
come,
let us search for everything
you lost in your youth

From now on
I will be
your mother
note: Subramania Bharathi is the Tamil poet of courage and defiance. Thirukkural 69 says a mother rejoices more on hearing her son called a learned man than on the day he was born; the poet asks his mother not to wait for that.
